\(a \equiv b \pmod n\) means: When does a have an inverse mod n?
n divides a - b. Same remainder on divis: Exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1. Bezout gives it.
If p is prime and p does not divide a, then \(a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p\).

\(a \equiv b \pmod n\) means: Key idea in the proof of Fermat
n divides a - b. Same remainder on divis: Multiplying 1, 2, ..., p-1 by a just shuffles them mod p. Compare products and cancel (p-1)!.
Mod p - 1 (for a prime modulus p and a coprime base), not mod p.

\(a \equiv b \pmod n\) means: Why can you not divide by 2 mod 6?
n divides a - b. Same remainder on divis: gcd(2, 6) = 2. Times 2 collides: 1 and 4 both go to 2.
A composite n like 561 = 3·11·17 with \(a^{n-1} \equiv 1\) for every a coprime to n. It fools the Fermat test.
